lessons.title: What a fraction means
lessons.why: Fractions let us describe equal shares, probabilities, averages and measurements. Today we only need equal parts.
explanation: Choose one whole and split it into equal-sized parts. The denominator counts how many such parts make one whole. The numerator counts how many you take.
For 1/3, split a rectangle into three equal pieces and shade one. Two rectangles of different whole sizes need not represent equal amounts even if both say 1/3.
Split each third into two equal parts. The same shaded amount is now 2/6, so 1/3 = 2/6. The amount stays the same; only its name changes.
A denominator cannot be zero: division by zero does not describe a valid equal partition. You do not need decimals, negative numbers or powers today.

worked_example.text: One of three equal pieces is 1/3. Split all three pieces in half: two of six equal pieces are shaded, so 1/3 = 2/6.

lessons.practice: On paper, draw 2/3 of a rectangle. Label the top and bottom numbers. Draw 1/2 and 3/6 using the same-sized whole.
lessons.discovery: Repartition your own drawing. Give the same shaded amount two fraction names. Explain the equal-parts rule.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
lessons.why: We can combine shares only after expressing them in the same-sized pieces.
explanation: For 1/4 + 2/4, the pieces have the same size. Count three quarters: 3/4.
For 1/2 + 1/4, first split the half into two quarters. Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.
The denominator describes the size of the pieces; adding it would silently change the unit. Subtraction uses the same common-unit idea.

worked_example.text: 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. A whole plus nothing is still a whole; 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, which refutes adding numerators and denominators together.

lessons.practice: Draw and calculate 1/3 + 1/6. Then 3/4 − 1/4. Explain which pieces you counted.
lessons.discovery: Construct a counterexample to “add tops and add bottoms.” Say exactly why it fails.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
lessons.why: Multiplication can describe a part of a part. Division asks how many units of one amount fit in another.
explanation: Half of three quarters is three eighths: (1/2) × (3/4) = 3/8. Draw a rectangle split in both directions.
How many quarter-units fit in a half? Two, so (1/2) ÷ (1/4) = 2.
Dividing by a nonzero fraction equals multiplying by its reciprocal. Numerator/denominator cancellation needs genuine common factors; never cancel across a sum.
lessons.practice: Calculate (2/3) × (3/5) and (1/2) ÷ (1/4). Draw the second as a counting question.
lessons.discovery: Can dividing a positive number make it larger? Give an example and explain the unit being counted.

lessons.why: Decimals are a place-value notation for tenths, hundredths and smaller equal parts.
explanation: 0.3 means three tenths: 3/10. 0.25 means twenty-five hundredths: 25/100 = 1/4.

lessons.title: Ratios, rates and percentages
lessons.why: A comparison is meaningful only when we know which quantities and units it compares.
explanation: With 2 red tokens and 3 blue tokens, red:blue is 2:3. Red as a fraction of all tokens is 2/5, because there are five tokens in total.

Percent means per hundred. 25% = 25/100 = 1/4, so 25% of 80 equals 20. The reference amount matters.

lessons.title: Negative numbers and signed operations
lessons.why: Negative numbers extend the number line so that subtraction and directional changes can be described consistently.
explanation: Place zero on a line. Positive numbers lie to its right; negative numbers lie to its left. −2 is greater than −5 because it lies further right.
Starting at −2 and moving five units right gives −2 + 5 = 3. Subtracting three from two gives 2 − 3 = −1.
Multiplication sign rules must agree with distribution and additive inverses. For example, 0 = (−2)×(3 + (−3)) forces (−2)×(−3) = 6. Divide only by nonzero numbers.
lessons.practice: Draw −3 and −1, then calculate −4 + 6, 3 − 8 and (−3)×(−2). Explain each direction/sign.
lessons.discovery: Create two examples where a number with a larger absolute magnitude is actually smaller.

lessons.title: Powers and grouping
lessons.why: Exponent notation compresses repeated multiplication. Grouping determines which operation acts on which value.
explanation: 3² means 3×3 = 9. It does not mean 3×2.
Do grouped operations first, then powers, then multiplication/division from left to right, then addition/subtraction from left to right.
2 + 3×4 = 14, while (2+3)×4 = 20. −(2²) = −4, while (−2)² = 4. Zero/negative exponents and roots remain separate later lessons.

worked_example.text: 2³ = 2×2×2 = 8. Parentheses make the base explicit: (−3)² = 9, while −(3²) = −9.

lessons.title: Variables, expressions and equations
lessons.why: Algebra lets us describe a calculation or relationship without fixing every number in advance.
explanation: In this lesson a variable is a symbol for a number. An expression, such as 3x+2, represents a value. An equation, such as 3x+2=14, states equality.
To evaluate an expression, replace each occurrence of a variable by the given number, keeping grouping clear. At x=4, 3x+2 = 3×4+2 = 14.
In Python, = assigns a value to a name; it does not solve an algebraic equation.

worked_example.text: At z=3, 5z+1 = 16. The expression 5z+1 and the equation 5z+1=16 play different roles.

lessons.practice: Evaluate 2x+1 at x=0 and x=4. Write an expression describing three groups of a number plus two.
lessons.discovery: Compare (x+2)+3 with x+5. Explain why two examples alone do not prove an identity for every x.

lessons.title: Preserving equality
lessons.why: Solving an equation means finding values that make its equality true, while keeping equivalent conditions.
explanation: For x+5=12, subtract 5 from both sides to obtain x=7. Check by substitution: 7+5=12.
Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides preserves the solution set. Multiplication/division by a nonzero number is reversible.
Multiplication by zero can lose information. Division by zero is undefined. Learn distribution and equations on both sides later through MAT-ALG.

worked_example.text: For t+3=11, subtract 3 from both sides: t=8. Substitution checks the result.

lessons.practice: Solve x−4=9 and 3x=18. Explain why your operation preserves the same solutions.
lessons.discovery: Show how changing only one side can destroy equality using a numerical example.
